html:
From the 12th century to 1949 the narrow coast of Kerala, between the Western Ghats and the sea, was divided among small kingdoms that lived on the pepper trade.

The old Chera kingdom broke up about 1124. Three powers came out of it:

  • Calicut in the north, under a ruler called the Zamorin. He welcomed Arab merchants, and by 1400 his port was the main pepper market of the Indian Ocean. The Chinese admiral Zheng He called there and died there in 1433.
  • Cochin in the middle, Calicut's weaker rival.
  • Venad in the south, later Travancore.

Vasco da Gama landed near Calicut in 1498. The Zamorin fought the Portuguese at sea for a century, while Cochin took their side and became their base, and later the Dutch one.

In the 18th century King Marthanda Varma of Travancore conquered the south and beat a Dutch force at Colachel in 1741. Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan of Mysore overran the north after 1766, and it passed to the British in 1792.

Travancore and Cochin lasted as princely states, known for schools and high literacy. They merged in 1949, and Kerala state was formed in 1956. See also the Saint Thomas Christians and Islam on the Malabar coast.
sum: From the 12th century to 1949 the narrow coast of Kerala, between the Western Ghats and the sea, was divided among small kingdoms that lived on the pepper trade.
